Q: Determine if argument into method is "self" A:

I think @Matthew_Story's answer explains the solution well.

However, one crucial aspect of this solution (as mentioned in the answer) is that for Python 3.X you must instantiate the class to get the bound method, i.e., inspect.ismethod(Foo.bar) will return False, and only inspect.ismethod(Foo().bar) will return True.

For anybody coming to this and wondering (as I did), "how would I do this if instantiating the class is difficult?", for instance, because the constructor (i.e., __init__ method) takes arguments that are more effort to provide than what it's worth. One way you can solve this is by using the __new__ method to create an instance without having to call __init__ and properly construct the object. Adapting the example from the question (with no default for the bias parameter), this would then become:

>>> import inspect
>>> class TestNode(object):
...     def __init__(what, bias):
...         what.bias = bias
...     def update(what, t, x):
...         return t / x * what.bias
...
... inst = object.__new__(TestNode)
... inspect.ismethod(inst.update)
True

Note that we did not need to provide a value for the bias parameter to instantiate the TestNode object, despite it having no default.

I should note that in general it is not a good idea to directly use the __new__ method. However in this case, since we are not planning on actually using the instantiated object, it would be acceptable.

Q: Indexing a 1D Numpy array using 2D array A:

What array array indexing rule applies to following code?

That's how numpy's advanced indexing works. The shape of result array is related to shape of index array, the array's shape and the axis you're passing the index. Here are some examples that passes a 3D array as index to the first axis of arrays with different shapes.

In [47]: a.shape
Out[47]: (2, 5)

In [48]: b = a[np.array([[[0],[1]],[[1],[1]]])]

In [49]: b.shape
Out[49]: (2, 2, 1, 5)

In [50]: arr.shape
Out[50]: (3, 3, 3)

In [51]: b = arr[np.array([[[0],[1]],[[1],[1]]])]

In [52]: b.shape
Out[52]: (2, 2, 1, 3, 3)

And here is what you get when you pass different arrays to different axises:

In [61]: b = arr[[[0],[2]],[[1],[0]]]

In [62]: b.shape
Out[62]: (2, 1, 3)

In [63]: arr.shape
Out[63]: (3, 3, 3)

In all of these indexings, Numpy will check multiple things, first off, it checks the type of the objects passed as index. Secondly, it compares the shapes of your index array with the shape of respective axis of your array. Thirdly, it checks if the result produces a valid Numpy array.

Here are some other examples:

In [64]: b = arr[[[[0],[2]]],[[1],[0]]]

In [65]: b.shape
Out[65]: (1, 2, 1, 3)

In [66]: b
Out[66]: 
array([[[[ 3,  4,  5]],

        [[18, 19, 20]]]])

In [67]: b = arr[[[[0],[2]]],[1],[0]]

In [68]: b
Out[68]: 
array([[[ 3],
        [21]]])

Q: Converting non-constant wide character strings to multibyte character strings, C not C++ A:

The parameter OP is concerned with is not declared pointer to const; it is pointer to pointer to const, and that is not implicitly converted from a pointer to a pointer to non-const.
